title: The Saturated Star
subtitle: Why the brightest star in the frame has the wrong magnitude, what bleeding and cosmic rays do to its neighbors, and where a measurement is safe
body:
Step 1 of 9 read

The brightest star in the frame

A CCD records light by collecting electrons in each pixel, and a pixel can hold only so many: the full well, 50,000 electrons here. The frame below shows one very bright star, S, among fainter ones. The photometry tool measures each star and, when it cannot trust a number, it refuses and says why: the stars drawn in orange are the ones it refused.

The frame is synthetic: made by a model, with the star brightnesses and the electrons they put on the frame known exactly. Nobody observed it.

subtitle: Why the brightest star in the frame has the wrong magnitude, what bleeding and cosmic rays do to its neighbors, and where a measurement is safe

What would the number have been?

The tool refuses S. Suppose it had not: it adds up the light in a circle around the star, as it does for every other star. The row for S says what it would have read, as a share of the electrons the model put in.

Added up anyway, the flux of S would be…

title: The Saturated Star
subtitle: Why the brightest star in the frame has the wrong magnitude, what bleeding and cosmic rays do to its neighbors, and where a measurement is safe
body:
Step 9 of 9 read

What an observer does

What you saw comes to one point: a quality flag is a refusal, and the refusal is the safe answer. A saturated star is avoided with a shorter exposure or a defocused star, and measured where it does not saturate. A star a cosmic ray crosses is recovered by combining several exposures with rejection. And a flagged pixel is never corrected by hand: it is replaced by a better image. The frames are synthetic and the effects are stated models, not a measured detector.
